clinicalPearls: A rare cause of agammaglobulinaemia with a profound early B-cell maturation block, clinically resembling X-linked agammaglobulinaemia but inherited autosomal recessively and affecting both sexes.

Caused by biallelic defects in components of the pre-B-cell receptor or its signalling machinery, most often the immunoglobulin mu heavy chain (IGHM), with rarer defects in IGLL1 (lambda 5/surrogate light chain), CD79A, CD79B, BLNK and PIK3R1.

Presents with recurrent bacterial infections (otitis, sinusitis, pneumonia) once transplacental maternal IgG wanes, typically earlier and more severely than in X-linked disease for the mu heavy-chain form.
Hallmark laboratory picture is absent or profoundly reduced circulating B cells (CD19/CD20) with markedly low immunoglobulins of all classes, while T-cell numbers and function are preserved.
Absence of tonsils and palpable lymph nodes on examination reflects the failure of B-lineage development, an important clinical clue.
Mu heavy-chain deficiency tends to cause the most complete block and the most severe early phenotype among the autosomal recessive forms.
Management centres on lifelong immunoglobulin replacement and prompt antimicrobial treatment; live vaccines should be avoided.
A family history of consanguinity or affected siblings of either sex, with a normal BTK gene, should prompt consideration of an autosomal recessive cause.
reference.pathophysiology: Autosomal recessive agammaglobulinaemia arises from biallelic loss-of-function defects in molecules essential for assembly and signalling of the pre-B-cell receptor, the checkpoint that permits progression from the pro-B to pre-B stage in the bone marrow. The commonest culprit is the immunoglobulin mu heavy chain (IGHM); other genes include IGLL1 encoding the lambda 5 surrogate light chain, the signal-transducing Ig-alpha and Ig-beta chains (CD79A, CD79B), the cytosolic adaptor BLNK, and PIK3R1. Because the pre-B-cell receptor cannot form or transmit its survival and proliferation signal, developing B-lineage cells fail to progress and undergo apoptosis, producing a near-complete absence of mature circulating B cells and germinal centres. Without B cells there is no differentiation into plasma cells, so all immunoglobulin isotypes are profoundly deficient and specific antibody responses are absent. T-cell development, which proceeds independently in the thymus, is intact, so cellular immunity and lymphocyte counts driven by T cells remain normal, distinguishing this from combined immunodeficiencies. The consequent humoral failure leaves the patient susceptible to encapsulated pyogenic bacteria and to enteroviral infection once protective maternal IgG is catabolised in infancy.
additionalDifferentials: Common variable immunodeficiency with very low B cells
Rituximab or other B-cell-depleting drug effect
additionalInvestigations: Serum immunoglobulin quantification (IgG, IgA, IgM) with age-matched interpretation
Lymphocyte immunophenotyping showing absent CD19/CD20 B cells with preserved T and NK cells
Specific antibody titres to prior vaccines and isohaemagglutinins
BTK protein expression and BTK gene testing to exclude X-linked disease
Targeted or panel gene sequencing (IGHM, IGLL1, CD79A, CD79B, BLNK, PIK3R1)
Bone marrow examination showing arrest at the pro-B to pre-B transition
Screening for chronic enteroviral infection when neurological features arise
redFlags: Overwhelming or recurrent invasive bacterial infection in infancy after maternal antibody wanes
Chronic enteroviral meningoencephalitis with progressive neurological decline
Failure to thrive with recurrent respiratory infections and absent lymphoid tissue
Bronchiectasis developing from repeated or inadequately treated pneumonia
Any live vaccine administration in a child with suspected agammaglobulinaemia
reference.prognosis: With early diagnosis, lifelong immunoglobulin replacement and prompt treatment of infections, long-term survival and quality of life are generally good. Delayed diagnosis, established bronchiectasis or chronic enteroviral infection substantially worsen the outlook.
pitfalls: Assuming all agammaglobulinaemia is X-linked and stopping the work-up when BTK is normal, missing an autosomal recessive gene
Overlooking the diagnosis in a female child because agammaglobulinaemia is wrongly regarded as a male-only disease
Misreading low immunoglobulins in early infancy as physiological before B cells are enumerated
Administering live vaccines before immune status is established
Attributing recurrent infection to poor adherence rather than searching for the underlying B-cell defect
management: Lifelong immunoglobulin replacement, given intravenously or subcutaneously, is the mainstay and should maintain protective trough IgG levels
Treat bacterial infections promptly and aggressively with appropriate antibiotics, and use antibiotic prophylaxis in selected patients
Avoid live attenuated vaccines, which are unsafe and ineffective, and ensure close contacts are appropriately immunised
Monitor for and manage chronic sinopulmonary disease and bronchiectasis with airway clearance, physiotherapy and early treatment of exacerbations
Maintain vigilance for chronic enteroviral infection, a serious complication of the antibody deficiency
Review immunoglobulin trough levels, growth and end-organ function at regular immunology follow-up
Provide genetic counselling and family screening, noting autosomal recessive inheritance affecting both sexes
